extracted.intended_audience: linguists, humor researchers, graduate students and scholars in pragmatics/cognitive linguistics/corpus linguistics
extracted.subtask_description: Overview and evaluative criteria for analyzing verbal humor from semantic, pragmatic, discourse, and corpus perspectives; presents major theories (SSTH, GTVH), methodological guidance for corpus work, and pragmatic/conversational functions of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal vs. Referential humor (de dicto / de re)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between humor “de re” and “de dicto”: referential (de re) is purely semantic/pragmatic and does not depend on the linguistic form (the signifier), whereas verbal (de dicto) crucially depends on the signifier (puns, ambiguity-based humor, repetition of parts of the signifier such as alliteration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: verbal humor includes puns, homonymy, paronymy, etc., which exploit the signifier to bring together incongruous semantic/pragmatic meanings; referential humor relies only on semantic/pragmatic incongruity (example: homophony between [red] and [read]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity and (playful) resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often involves an incongruity between meanings which is then playfully 'resolved'—the resolution is para-logical and non-serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should identify the incongruous elements and how the text permits an overlapping or reinterpretation that justifies both meanings; note that 'resolution' is not literal logical reconciliation but a playful semantic/pragmatic closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic-Script Theory of Humor (SSTH): two conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Raskin's SSTH necessary and sufficient conditions for a text to be funny: (1) the text is compatible, fully or in part, with two different scripts; (2) the two scripts with which the text is compatible are opposite in a special sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SSTH to detect script compatibility and oppositions; caution that SSTH encodes a complex semantic theory beyond the two pithy conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSTH as a competence theory (not performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: SSTH is explicitly a theory of a speaker's competence (the potential of a text to be perceived as humorous), not of performance (whether a particular person in a particular context actually finds it funny).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying SSTH, evaluate the text's potential across competent speakers rather than relying on individual reactions; misfires in reception do not falsify SSTH applicability to a text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of semantics/pragmatics boundary; non-bona-fide communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Raskin denies the usefulness of a strict semantics/pragmatics divide and introduces 'non-bona-fide communication' to characterize non-cooperative (humorous) exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should treat semantic and pragmatic information jointly and consider humor as a type of non-cooperative (non-bona-fide) interaction (e.g., flouting Gricean maxims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Script opposition (GTVH knowledge resource)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of six GTVH knowledge resources: the script opposition (inherited from SSTH) that underpins the incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the opposing scripts that the text evokes; this is a top-level resource in GTVH and conditions lower-level choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical mechanism (GTVH knowledge resource)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH knowledge resource: the logical mechanism handling the resolution of the incongruity introduced by the script opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify how the joke resolves the incongruity (e.g., via analogy, absurdity, punning mechanism) as part of the logical-mechanism analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation (GTVH knowledge resource)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH knowledge resource: the situation or environment in which the humorous narrative takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe contextual/situational parameters that license particular script oppositions or targets (e.g., social setting, roles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Target (GTVH knowledge resource)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH knowledge resource: the target, i.e., the butt of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify who/what is mocked or targeted (social groups, stereotypes); target choice affects perceived similarity and social function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative strategy (GTVH knowledge resource)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH knowledge resource: the narrative strategy — how the text is organized (e.g., series structure; two normal occurrences followed by a deviant third).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse macro-structure (punch-line placement, series patterns, jab lines) and how narrative strategy creates expectations or breaks them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (GTVH knowledge resource)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH knowledge resource: the linguistic choices with which other components are verbalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document specific lexical, syntactic, phonological, and rhetorical devices used to realize the joke (wordplay, register mixing, hyperbole, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical organization of GTVH knowledge resources
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH claim: the six knowledge resources are hierarchically organized so that choices in higher (more abstract) resources affect choices in lower ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing jokes, consider which knowledge resources differ; differences at higher levels (e.g., script opposition) produce greater perceived dissimilarity than differences at lower levels (e.g., language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch line vs. jab line and joke positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Short jokes tend to place the script opposition at the end (punch line); in longer texts, script oppositions occur throughout and Attardo introduced 'jab line' to mark non-final humorous occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish text-final punch lines from jab lines distributed across narratives; analyse distribution statistically where possible (e.g., Corduas et al. findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of verbal devices (puns, homonymy, paronymy, alliteration, repetition, metaphors, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic humor includes puns, ambiguity-based humor, repetition of signifier parts (alliteration), homonymy (homophones/homographs), paronymy (partial homonymy), metaphorical literalization, metonymy, conceptual blending, forced reinterpretation (trumping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use taxonomic distinctions (paradigmatic vs. syntagmatic; homonymy types) to classify forms of verbal humor; note that early research focused heavily on such taxonomic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic theories of irony and sarcasm (multiple models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several pragmatic accounts of irony exist: (1) standard pragmatic model (Grice/Searle) — irony as flout of a maxim; (2) direct access theory (Gibbs) — direct access to ironic meaning; (3) graded salience theory (Giora) — most salient meaning first; (4) mention theory (Sperber & Wilson) — irony as echo/mention with critical stance; (5) pretense theory — speaker pretends to be another speaker expressing the utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these competing accounts to explain ironic/sarcastic utterances; empirical evidence (psycholinguistic, corpus) may favor different models in different contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast account of irony
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing consensus frames irony as involving contrast between expected/preferred state and observed state; contrast subsumes pretense, mention, and standard models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrast as a unifying analytic tool linking irony accounts with script-opposition accounts of humor; analyze how expectations are highlighted or negated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social functions of humor (solidarity, exclusion, identity work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor serves disparate social functions: pro-socially to build in-group solidarity, and anti-socially to exclude and denigrate targets; functions vary with setting (workplace, friends, classroom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humorous interaction, assess intended and realized social functions (bonding, teasing, subversion), and consider whether humor creates in-group/out-group divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor support strategies and mode adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor support consists of discursive strategies acknowledging/supporting humorous turns: laughter, echoing, increased backchanneling, producing more humor; mode adoption is adopting the speaker's mode (e.g., responding ironically to ironic utterance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify supportive moves and measure degrees of adoption vs. mere appreciation; mode adoption is a stronger form of solidarity than simple laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-stage hearer processing for humor (recognize, understand, appreciate, react)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hay's model: the hearer must (1) recognize the intention to produce humor, (2) understand the humor stimulus, (3) appreciate the humor, and (4) react — with each stage implicationally dependent on the previous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sequence to diagnose failed humor (failure can occur at any stage); empirical analysis should try to observe which stage fails (e.g., recognition without understanding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failed humor: identification and importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Failed humor is crucial methodologically because it cannot be identified solely by laughter/smiling; reactions range from ignoring to strong criticism, and causes map onto communicative misunderstandings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should include failed humor in corpora analyses to avoid biasing results toward successful humor; use contextual/intentional evidence to detect attempted but unrecognized humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decommitment (retractability) and use of humor to test risky behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractability or decommitment (the ability to discount one's remarks as non-serious, 'just kidding') lets speakers test socially risky behavior and challenge authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse instances of decommitment as interactional devices for negotiating face and power; in workplaces this can both reinforce and subvert power differentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus methodology: representativeness, size, and balanced corpora
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpora allow frequency-based generalizations but only if representative of the population of interest; size and balance predict validity of inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using corpus data for humor research, document corpus design, sampling frame, and balance; small or unrepresentative corpora limit generalizability (Holmes, Partington examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of humor in corpora: triangulation using paralinguistic, semantic/pragmatic, and metalinguistic cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Holmes' proposed definition: 'utterances which are identified by the analyst, on the basis of paralinguistic, prosodic and discoursal clues, as intended by the speaker(s) to be amusing and perceived to be amusing by at least some participants.' Attardo suggests triangulating Holmes' cues with semantic/pragmatic models (GTVH) and metalinguistic markers to detect unacknowledged humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on laughter; combine prosodic/paralinguistic evidence with semantic/pragmatic script analysis and any available participant-reported perceptions to identify humor (including unacknowledged instances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter and smiling are unreliable sole markers of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter may occur without humor and humor may occur without laughter; prosodic marking of punch/jab lines is often absent in naturalistic data; smiling intensity may correlate with humor more consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat laughter/smiling/prosody as partial indicators; prefer multimodal triangulation (facial expression, prosody, discourse context). Report rates of false positives/negatives if using laughter as proxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal and audiovisual corpora for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving to audiovisual and multimodal corpora (video + audio + transcriptions) enables analysis of facial, prosodic, and bodily markers of humor; recent work shows surprising findings (e.g., punch lines often unmarked prosodically; smiling more indicative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multimodal data where possible; analyze correlations between visual markers (smile intensity), prosody, and instances of humor; be cautious about assuming prosodic marking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keying/framing is independent of humor (deadpan, a posteriori keying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keying/framing a situation as humorous is not a prerequisite for humor: un-keyed (deadpan) humor exists, and situations can be keyed a posteriori after an initially un-keyed humorous event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming that a frame must precede humorous recognition; investigate whether keying occurs before or after participants recognize the humor and how that affects interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variationist dimensions to evaluate (gender, ethnicity, age, class, national differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor varies across social dimensions; research is uneven (gender studied more, others less); corpus results sometimes overturn earlier assumptions (e.g., women producing more humor in some corpora).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include demographic and social variables in analyses where relevant; do not generalize from one population without checking variation across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic markers and authorial humor signature
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic analyses (corpus-assisted) can differentiate an author's humorous style (e.g., Wodehouse: mixture of formal and colloquial style, use of hyperbole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use corpus stylistic methods to extract features that characterize humorous style: register mixing, frequency of hyperbole, lexical patterns, etc.; report distinguishing features quantitatively when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and performance: prosodic timing often absent
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies of timing in joke performance find that speakers do not reliably prosodically mark punch lines or jab lines (no consistent higher pitch, volume, pauses); laughter is not reliably adjacent to humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing timing/performance, document prosodic measures but expect sparse marking; combine timing analysis with other modalities (facial, gestural) and discourse structure.
